name: Liftbridge
workload: Single-node Liftbridge cluster (replication factor 1) publishing messages with 4 concurrent publishers and pub-batch=100, file storage, using the repo's own bench/producer tool.
claimed_speedup: ~241K msgs/sec (4 publishers, pub-batch=100, file storage, RF=1) vs NATS JetStream's ~220K msgs/sec at similar settings (pubbatch=100, file storage, RF=1) - about 1.1x higher throughput
tradeoffs: Go implementation layered on NATS Streaming/JetStream semantics rather than Kafka's; simpler ops story but a much smaller ecosystem/tooling base than Kafka; only one config point (RF=1, single node) is benchmarked.
caveats: No hardware/CPU model, OS, or message size stated for either side of the comparison; figures are the project's own self-reported numbers, not an independently reproduced side-by-side run.
found_via: Blogs/talks: gh search code (README performance-claim search for Kafka/NATS comparisons) -> liftbridge-io/liftbridge README 'Performance' section

name: msgq (comma.ai)
workload: 1 KiB message cross-process ping-pong on x86 Linux; msgq compared against pyzmq (ZeroMQ) IPC, multiprocessing.Pipe, Eclipse Zenoh IPC, and LCM UDP backends using the repo's own benchmarks/examples/benchmark.py harness.
claimed_speedup: 362.13k msgs/sec (msgq) vs 113.97k msgs/sec (pyzmq/ZeroMQ IPC) - about 3.2x higher throughput (derived from page data: bar chart embedded in README)
hardware: x86 Linux (exact CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 256 stars; used in production in comma.ai's openpilot
tradeoffs: Single-host IPC only (no network transport like real ZeroMQ/Kafka); ring-buffer based pub/sub, not a durable/distributed log; C/C++ core with Python bindings, so Python overhead is included in the benchmark on both sides.
caveats: Benchmark code is public and runnable, but the README only states 'x86 Linux' with no CPU model, kernel version, or compiler flags, so this falls short of Tier A/B despite being reproducible; compares against pyzmq (Python ZeroMQ bindings) rather than a native C++ ZeroMQ client.
found_via: Blogs/talks: gh search repos 'pub sub' language:C++ sort:stars -> commaai/msgq README benchmark chart (image downloaded and read directly)

name: High-performance pub/sub (uWS broadcast-coalescing prototype)
workload: Broadcast-coalescing pub/sub prototype built on uWebSockets, tested against an equivalent Redis pub/sub implementation for the same fan-out problem size (exact message count/size not stated in the README).
claimed_speedup: Completes in 89 ms vs Redis pub/sub's 5 s for the same problem size - 'more than 50x faster than Redis pub/sub' (README also claims >3000x vs a Socket.IO based implementation, 4.5 min)
tradeoffs: Single C++11 'braindump' file demonstrating a broadcast-batching technique on top of uWebSockets, not a full message broker (no persistence, clustering, or wire-protocol compatibility); problem size and hardware are unspecified so the ratio can't be independently checked.
caveats: No hardware, message size/count, or test setup given for either side; the >50x and >3000x speedups with no stated methodology are capped at tier C per the hard rules (implausible ratio, unstated flags); appears to be a mirrored 2016 write-up by uWebSockets author Alex Hultman rather than an original repo.
found_via: Blogs/talks: gh search repos 'pub sub' language:C++ sort:stars -> skyformat99/High-performance-pub-sub README

name: Fero
workload: Single-node fero server + client, fire-and-round-trip-ack of a single message repeated 10,000 times (tests/integration/speed/latency/client); separate throughput test sends 1M messages of 10/100/1000 bytes (tests/integration/speed/sync), modeled on LinkedIn's published Kafka benchmark methodology, and compared against Kafka's and ZeroMQ's own reported latency/throughput figures.
claimed_speedup: Median round-trip latency 0.06ms (fero) vs Kafka's reported 2ms (~33x), 99th pct 0.3ms vs 3ms (~10x), 99.9th pct 1.86ms vs 14ms (~7.5x); ZeroMQ's one-way average latency cited as ~0.06ms (comparable); throughput at 100-byte messages ~72MB/s (fero) vs LinkedIn's reported ~75MB/s for Kafka (roughly on par, fero slightly behind) (derived from page data)
hardware: Dell XPS 15 9550, Intel Core i7-6700HQ @ 2.60GHz, 4-core/8-thread, 32GB RAM, Windows 10, Node.js v8.0.0 (fero side only; the cited Kafka/ZeroMQ numbers come from LinkedIn's separately-run, multi-machine Kafka benchmark, not a side-by-side run on the same hardware)
tradeoffs: Node.js, single-process-per-node design (no JVM); application-layer sharding via consistent hashring instead of Kafka's fixed partitions/ZooKeeper; author calls the project 'very experimental'; no multi-node clustering benchmark published, no disk-durability model directly comparable to Kafka's log.
caveats: Kafka figures are pulled from LinkedIn's separately-published, multi-machine Kafka benchmark rather than measured on the same hardware as fero's laptop test, so this is an indirect, apples-to-oranges comparison; no license file in the repo (treat as reference-only, do not copy the code); project unmaintained since 2018.
found_via: Blogs/talks: gh search code '"faster than kafka" in README' filename:README.md -> pemrouz/fero README 'Performance' section

name: Harper (formerly HarperDB)
language: JavaScript (unverified - Harper's source is not public; only the benchmark harness is)
baseline: Apache Kafka (plus Postgres/Redis/Debezium/Kafka Streams ecosystem, workload-dependent)
workload: Four workloads run on identical single-VM hardware (24GB RAM / 8 vCPU): (W1) durable write + downstream notify, (W2) filtered fan-out messaging to subscriber subsets, (W3) 5-minute windowed running-total analytics plus point lookups, (W4) sustained log ingestion at 1,000 events/sec. Conventional stack = Kafka (+ Postgres + Debezium + Redis + Kafka Streams as needed per workload) tuned idiomatically (acks=all, lz4, batched) vs a single Harper cluster with matched durability guarantees.
claimed_speedup: W1: p50 9ms vs 876ms (~100x); W2: p50 12.5ms vs 165ms (~13x); W3 freshness: p50 1.05s vs 3.65s (~3x); W4: p50 1.4ms vs 57ms (~40x); Kafka Streams wins the W3 point-lookup case: 2.75ms (Kafka) vs 17ms (Harper) (~6x Kafka faster) (all verbatim from the repo README results table)
hardware: Single laptop VM, 24GB RAM, 8 vCPU (exact CPU model not stated)
license: Elastic-2.0 for the Harper Pro container image under test (source-available, non-OSI); the benchmark harness code in this repo is Apache-2.0
stars_or_usage: 0 stars on the benchmark repo; Harper is a commercially-backed database/streaming product
tradeoffs: Harper itself is closed/source-available (pulled as a pinned Docker image, not built from public source in this repo), so only the benchmark harness is inspectable, not the system under test; single-VM test bed, not a multi-node production comparison; author is openly Harper-affiliated.
caveats: Author explicitly discloses Harper affiliation and solicits independent Kafka-SME audits; tested on a single laptop VM only (README calls this 'the largest known limitation' and explicitly says the W4 result is 'a laptop-VM artifact, not a system limit', not Kafka's real throughput ceiling); no exact CPU model given; the ~100x and ~40x results exceed the 50x implausibility threshold so tier is capped at C per the hard rules even though the methodology docs (methodology.md, decisions.md) are unusually thorough and transparent about limitations.
found_via: Blogs/talks: gh search code 'beats Kafka' filename:README.md -> HarperFast/kafka-v-harper-perf-test README
